This section examines Chapter 5 —
Convergence theory, carefully stated

(8–10 minutes) from first principles. Keep
two questions separate: does

changing the order change the measured
outcome, and does the

proposed search method beat a matched
alternative at the same

distinct-evaluation budget? Build the
Markov-chain argument in this order: A

state is the entire population, not one
permutation. The state

space consists of multisets of mu
permutations from S_n. Selection,

mutation, and replacement define
transition probabilities. A population

containing an optimum is an absorbing
state under elitist replacement.

Positive mutation probability and a
connected mutation graph make the

optimum reachable. Display and narrate the
almost-sure convergence

statement:
lim_{ttoinfty}Pr(X_tinOmega_{opt})=1.

eventual guarantee, not a promise of fast
practical convergence. Then

introduce the paper’s expected-time
expression using the fundamental matrix:

mathbb{E}[T]=mathbf{1}^{top}(I-Q)^{-1}mathbf{1}.
Present the paper’s

O(n^3log n) claim specifically in the
stated swap-mutation setting and

immediately attach the empirical
limitation: deceptive or

operator-mismatched landscapes can be
censored under realistic budgets. Do

not generalize the rate to every
objective. Finally show the

geometric picture: d(X_t,Omega_{opt})le
rho(Q)^t d(X_0,Omega_{opt}). Animate

the illustrative rho(Q)approx0.96 curve
and the paper’s calculation of

approximately 113 generations for a 99%
threshold. Label it as

the paper’s parameterized theoretical
illustration, not a universal

constant. Add an optional technical
sidebar explaining that aging

replacement breaks population absorption
even if the best-ever record may

still converge; hybrid restart preserves
the best-ever ordering explicitly.

The distinction is part of the result. A
large ordering

effect does not automatically imply an
evolutionary-search advantage, and

almost-sure convergence does not promise
practical efficiency.
